text: Which game first introduced the concept of weapon recoil? Context This morning while watching a video of Wolfenstein 3D from 1992 and Doom (1993) I noticed that weapons don’t need to be compensated for any recoil. Then on my trip down memory lane I watched a Half Life (1998) video and there, automatic weapons at least seemed to have some form of recoil. There must have been something happening in between that introduced this feature into the game design of FPS, that is almost ubiquitous nowadays. Definition of recoil For the definition of recoil, I will use the definition used in the Counter Strike wiki , which I found to be a good summary of what I thought it is: Recoil is the backward momentum of a gun when it is discharging bullets and causes players' screens to "shake". This often causes the shooter to sway away from their intended target after the first shot due to the momentum "kicking" the shooter's aim. The higher the recoil, the more the screen will vibrate. To which I will add a picture to illustrate (CSGO recoil pattern of AK47): Which game introduced this concept of recoil when shooting and thus the compensation necessary to be accurate while shooting, say, full auto or rapidly, in an FPS?

All three are female, marking the first time an RPG videogame has offered an exclusively female line-up of heroes. Final Fantasy X-2 (13 March 2003) is therefore awarded the record for "First all-female ( MAIN PLAYABLE ) cast in an RPG videogame". This .... seems complete nonsense to me. Either the Guinness Record considered some other obscure requirements that aren't explicit in the record name or there is NO WAY FF X-2 is the first. Technically, there are also two support male characters that will join the party for a small part of the game, but those aren't controlled by the player in battle. Bishoujo Senshi Sailor Moon: Another Story (SNES, 1995) features all ten Sailor Senshi as playable characters. And since Mamoru / Tuxedo Mask isn't playable in any way, this time all the playable characters are indeed female. Therefore, I seriously doubt the Guinness Record claims can be believed under the expressed requirements. So this is my question: What was the first JRPG / RPG video game where every character the player could control at any time in the story was female?

text: What was the first game to voluntarily provide an in-game content warning? What was the first game to voluntarily provide an in-game content warning? If you grew up playing horror games, you've probably seen content warnings similar to this: This one is from Silent Hill , published in 1999. Basically, it's a voluntary self-declaration by the game that there's something objectionable presented in the game. What I'm looking for: The first voluntary message in a game outside of the game's internal narrative that warns the player about morally objectionable content in the game's story or presentation. Objectionable content is very commonly violent or sexual in nature, but it doesn't have to be. ( Assassin's Creed , for example, self-declared that its story could be considered culturally offensive.) The content warning could also be done tongue-in-cheek so long as it still performs the service of a content warning. (For example, God Hand featured a content warning for explicit violence and gore, which it certainly had, but it was first and foremost a jab at the content warnings at the beginning of Resident Evil games, which shared directors and publishers. It was also overlaid over a man getting kicked in the balls.) What I'm not looking for: Standardized warnings/descriptions required by government or commercial entities (ESRB, Videogame Rating Council, etc.). For the sake of having a tight upper bound, we won't accept anything required by the platform manufacturer. So, as in the above, a warning internally mandated by Konami for all Silent Hill games can be considered, but a warning required by Sony for all PlayStation 2 games cannot. In-game characters warning about objectionable content (for example, protestors in Postal 2 that object to events in the game). Warnings that focus on meta gameplay aspects rather than morally objectionable content (for example, Doom 's Nightmare difficulty displaying the message "Are you sure? This skill level isn't even remotely fair."). Warnings provided by advertisements, box art, cabinet art, and so forth. It has to be in the game.

text: Computers are deterministic 1 In mathematics, computer science and physics, a deterministic system is a system in which no randomness is involved in the development of future states of the system. A deterministic model will thus always produce the same output from a given starting condition or initial state. Deterministic Systems — Wikipedia Think of a computer like a cook who has been handed a recipe (a program) to bake a cake. Computers do not deviate from the instructions (input) in a program, meaning that each cake they bake (output) will be identical. So how do programs (including games) implement randomness? Comic #221: Random Number — xkcd A mathematical formula is used to "fake" randomness. This is known as a Pseudorandom Number Generator (PRNG), often abbreviated to just Random Number Generator (RNG). The problem is, being a mathematical formula — if you give it the same input value, you'll get the same output value. So what a PRNG does is feed the values it generates back into the formula to get more values, and so on. But we're left with a problem: What is the initial starting value? This is where the "seed" gets its name. It's a seed value , a number used to start the random number generator, so that it may generate future pseudo-random numbers. In most games, the seed is determined automatically using a few tricks, like deriving a value from the system clock, or the number of frames generated before user input. But this is also why clock manipulation or frame-counting are popular tactics in speedrunning circles — because they can take the "randomness" out of certain actions, to guarantee a more perfect run. Other games like Minecraft, which relies heavily on randomness for it's world generation, allow you to manually specify a seed to get the "same" world generation. Math/Comp-Sci crash course: Just for fun, let's look at a working example of a basic pseudorandom number generator 2 : Next_Value = (Multiplier * Current_Value + Increment) % Modulus The Modulo % operator gives us the remainder after division by the Modulus. For example, if 10 / 8 = 1 r2 , then 10 % 8 = 2 . We can use this as a limiter for the PRNG, as the remainder will always be less than the modulus. So let's set some values in the formula. A modulus of 101 will limit us to generating numbers between 0 and 100: Next_Value = (7 * Current_Value + 5) % 101 We need to seed Current_Value with something, so let's use a seed of 1 : Current Value Formula Next Value 1 (Seed) (7 * 1 + 5) % 101 12 12 (7 * 12 + 5) % 101 89 89 (7 * 89 + 5) % 101 22 22 (7 * 22 + 5) % 101 58 and now, let's try a seed of 42 : Current Value Formula Next Value 42 (Seed) (7 * 42 + 5) % 101 97 97 (7 * 97 + 5) % 101 78 78 (7 * 78 + 5) % 101 46 46 (7 * 46 + 5) % 101 24 As you can see, we're getting some "fake" random numbers, based off a seed value! Pretty cool, right? This is true for most computing applications you'll encounter day-to-day. In specialised cases (such as high-security applications) computers can act as non-deterministic systems by utilizing True Random Number Generators (TRNGs). These devices measure unpredictable physical phenomena (such as thermal noise or radioactive decay) to generate data that is truly random and not based on a formula. Non-deterministic behaviour may also be observed from situations such as multi-core processing (race conditions), hardware faults, or Single-Event Upsets (SEUs) (i.e. cosmic rays flipping bits, etc) This type of PRNG is known as a Linear Congruential Generator (LCG). There are other (more robust) PRNG formulas, this one just serves as a good simple example. This LCG will loop after about 100 iterations, and visit almost every number in the range 0-100, except 16. This is a consequence of the specific parameters chosen for the example. 16 is a "fixed point" for this specific equation (if you use 16 as the seed, you get 16 back: (7*16+5 = 117 -> 117%101 = 16)

text: Gachas are characterized by the fundamental way some, or all, of gameplay is gated: by a lootbox-adjacent mechanic. The difference between gachas and, say, Counter-Strike 2's lootboxes is that you may play all of what Counter-Strike 2 has to offer without ever opening a box, and not in a "technically, if you grind for 234 hours, you will be able to afford [weapon] for free" kind of way. The only things that are locked behind a loot box (however expensive it is to open) in Counter-Strike 2 are entirely cosmetic. For contrast, take the quintessential "gacha game": Genshin Impact. In Genshin Impact, to be able to play in a certain way, such as playing as a certain character, or using a certain weapon, the only way is to open a loot box. You may not buy the character from the shop directly. The only way to get what you want is to gamble. Sure, there are ways of gambling for free built into the game (this is a player retention mechanic, gachas are necessarly full of them otherwise they'd be extremely frustrating), but the fundamentals don't change: in order to experience the full game, or indeed any of the game at all, you must gamble. Some would argue that the entire purpose of the game is the gambling. Dragon Collection, one of the original gachas, was actually literally just a collection game with no gameplay attached. The entire point was to gamble to get the dragon you're missing from your collection. It was quite successful for a browser game of the era. Of course, this is a spectrum. Some games can be located somewhere in the middle, where most of the gameplay can genuinely be accessed for free, but the truly powerful elements are behind a lootbox wall. Also note that gacha games are not to be confused with so-called "freemium" games, where the game favors paid players much more than free-to-play ones. While the two are obviously related, the difference mostly comes down to the fact that freemium games almost always guarantee you will obtain something powerful by paying every time, while gachas hold no such guarantees and can very well reward you with "filler" items even after paying. In conclusion, gachas are defined not by "some amount of randomness in terms of player rewards", but large amounts of randomness in access to gameplay to begin with.

text: Short Answer: Enter the number "747" as the frequency to continue with the game. There is no way to find this information within the game (see full answer below). Full Answer: This is a question that one of my kids brought to me while playing the games that I grew up with, and - while you can find the following information on the internet - I thought it was worthy of documenting within Arqade. Interestingly, the method for getting the frequency has changed over the years. To be able to continue with the game requires knowledge of a 3-digit code that originally was included as a hidden message on a piece of paper that came with StarTropics when purchased new and unopened... 1990 Original NES Release From the original instruction manual: Notice the footnote in the bottom right corner: "Please read the letter from Dr. Jones appended to this booklet." Here is an image of the paper that was appended to the back ( image credit ): The basic gist of the letter is that Uncle Steve is responding to Mike and inviting him to visit him on C-Island. I will emphasize the extra words in the footnote at the bottom: "Note: This letter is very important so please hold onto it till the end of the game." As a kid, I remember thinking it was really cool to have this extra paper that was somehow important to the game. Now that we know about this physical letter, Baboo's cryptic message makes more sense. When the paper was made wet with water, a hidden message would appear ( image credit ): This was a real world component to a video game! Definitely a fun experience as a kid. Nowadays, you will likely buy the game used without the original packaging and manual - and crucial letter to Mike from Uncle Steve! The content of the secret message in the letter contributed to the whole secret spy feel: Uncle Steve felt as though he was being watched and took a precaution to put a "tiny transmitter in [his] shoe" which was tuned to the frequency of 747 MHz. 2008 Wii Virtual Console & 2016 Wii-U Virtual Console Releases When Nintendo released StarTropics for the Wii/Wii-U Virtual Console, they included an electronic version of the original letter in the Operations Guide, complete with a way to virtually "dip" the letter in water (by clicking on an image of a bucket of water) to reveal the necessary frequency: Here is a video of what it looked like to dip the letter on the Wii. (Thanks to @Showsni for the video link.) It is interesting to note that this virtual dipping only gave the minimum information to continue in the game (frequency 747 MHz), and did not include the hidden message from Uncle Steve revealing his (justified) paranoia and tiny transmitter. 2016 NES Classic Edition Release The NES Classic Edition release included two digital manuals, an " Electronic Manual " and a " Printed Manual ". The "Printed Manual" included the image of the blank letter. The "Electronic Manual" included a page to explain the letter and give the secret frequency: This gave all the same information as the original printed paper, complete with the secret message communicating Uncle Steve's spy-level precautions. 2019 Nintendo Switch Online Release When the game was released for the Nintendo Switch Online, they apparently omitted any copy of the letter (virtual, digital, or otherwise). Oops! Players who don't have any context to where that frequency was supposed to come from are forced to search online and find this answer: As we have learned from the above, the frequency that Nav-Com should tune to is 747 MHz. Entering this number will allow you to continue the game of StarTropics past Chapter 4.

text: Lane math is a strategy by which all lanes of connecting roads, usually highways and on/off-ramps end up matching. The goal is that each lane only goes to one specific direction. It is best explained by example: You have a 3-lane-highway and you want to make an exit and an on-ramp for it. Without lane math it will look like this: With lane math something like this: What changed? The highway has one less lane in the section between the off-ramp and on-ramp At the end of the off-ramp we switch two a two-lane-one-way so both left and right turn have a dedicated lane (ignore the arrow going straight, it is a possible path but it will never be used, as you wouldn't leave the highway just to rejoin it) The road has dedicated turn lanes to get onto the on-ramp What does it all do? When each lane only goes to one direction you avoid a lot of traffic. Say there are 4 cars at the end of the off-ramp waiting to turn left, but the road is full. If another car comes and wishes to turn right it has to wait in the top layout but can just go in the bottom one with lane math: The same applies for all other directions on the intersection. It also helps the highway itself with the right being a dedicated turn lane to the exit, cars will sort themself further up the highway into the correct lane. Thereby cars continuing on the highway will not be slowed down by cars braking for their exits (especially if the turn on the off-ramp is sharp this might be an issue). Should you ever have a congestion big enough to spill on the highway cars going somewhere else will not be affected. The same applies to the on-ramp. The right lane is, if you will, a continuation of the on-ramp and the cars from the highway will be on 2 other lanes thereby not slowed down by the still accelerating cars joining the highway. So is lane math important? High use roads definitely benefit from lane math as it clears/sorts traffic ahead of the actual interchanges. For low usage roads it might make little to no difference, but as your city grows usage might change so allways try to apply the correct lane math.

text: Because the original consideration was "what controls the opponent, and makes decisions for them?" In a PvP scenario, decisions for your opponent are made by another Player, with their brain, according to their strategy. In a PvE scenario, decisions are made by the computer, with its processor, according to the software instructions. The CPU is the part that does the calculations and supplies the next instruction, performing the role and player would. (In either case, "AI" is somewhat of an inaccurate buzzword, because there is no actual intelligence - however artificial - being displayed. "Simulated Intelligence" or "Faked Pseudo-Intelligence" would be better descriptions - but "CPU" remains more accurate than "AI")

text: This is the timeline of the games as we currently understand it † , according to official and unofficial sources : Main Timeline Skyward Sword ("Many years" later + 100 years) The Minish Cap ("Generations" later) Four Swords (After the Hylian civil war that lasted "a long time") Ocarina of Time / | \ Fallen Hero Timeline Child Timeline Adult Timeline ("Many years" later) A Link to the Past (Several months later) Majora's Mask ("Ages" + hundreds of years later) The Wind Waker (Soon after) Link's Awakening ("Many years" later) Twilight Princess (Soon after) Phantom Hourglass (Soon after) Oracle of Seasons/Ages (Hundreds of years later) Four Swords Adventures (One hundred years later) Spirit Tracks (Centuries later) A Link Between Worlds | | (Soon after) Triforce Heroes | | (An unknown amount of time later) Echoes of Wisdom * | | ("Many years" later) The Legend of Zelda | | (Six years later) The Adventure of Link | | (?)** (?)** (?)** Era of the Wilds/Great Calamity (Possibly more than 10,000 years later) Breath of the Wild * (Soon after) Tears of the Kingdom * The most confusing part is the timeline split after the events of Ocarina of Time . The quick explanation is that the Fallen Hero Timeline is the timeline where Link fails his quest and Ganon ends up with the completed Triforce, forcing the Sages to seal it and him within the Sacred Realm, which is now the Dark World. The Child Timeline is where Link successfully defeats Ganon and goes back in time as a child (i.e., the final scene of Ocarina of Time ). He warns Zelda about Ganondorf's betrayal and they prevent him from ever stealing the Triforce in the first place, though he survives his execution due to the gods giving him the Triforce of Power anyway ( for some reason ). The Adult Timeline stays in the future timeline after Link defeats Ganon. Because Link went back in time (to the Child Timeline), this timeline no longer has its Hero. So the next time Ganon appears, the gods are forced to intervene, resulting in the global flood. * : These games were released after the most recent official chronology update, so their place in the chronology is inferred from the in-game lore and might not be correct or might be retconned in the future. ** : It has been loosely confirmed that Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom take place at the end of one of the timelines, but which timeline specifically has apparently been left up to the imagination of the player . †: It is worth mentioning that according to The Legend of Zelda: Encyclopedia , the chronology of the Zelda games is not a high priority for Nintendo. They will maintain the timeline if practical, but they are also not afraid of breaking it for the sake of telling the story they want to tell for a specific game, and that ultimately the intention was always for the players themselves to create their own chronology according to their imagination. (Even the Encyclopedia itself states in its foreword that it was written with a certain amount of creative license to fill in some gaps.) So while the official timeline exists for the sake of convenience, it shouldn't be seen as an absolute truth.

text: In most traditional RTS's, the predominant factor in combat is concentration of force. Who can bring the stronger force to the combat will not only win the combat, but they will be able to inflict far more damage than weaker force. This encourages blobbing, because large concentrated blobs give a greater chance of achieving local force concentration superiority, whilst a spread out force opens up to losing the entire force through defeat in detail by an opponents blob. Not all RTS's follow this model. In particular Eugen Systems has a line (Wargame, Steel Division and WARNO) in RTS games that do form front-lines. Most of their mechanics contribute to it: Unlike traditional RTS's cover is hugely important. It grants significant damage reductions (to the point where combat is regularly decided based on which of the units involved are in cover). But it also increases stealth. This allows for slow glass canon units, which depending on positioning can be either massively strong or incredibly weak. These can be used to halt an enemy offense, but not be strong enough to attack themselves. Line of sight. Most units can only fire in line of sight, and the maps are designed to have a lot of clutter. This means the positioning units so you can fire but your opponent can't is a major part of the strategy. Lethal Combat: Higher damage levels can result in a lot of damage very quickly. A single unit can kill 5 enemy opponents in under a minute in the right circumstances. Lots of counters are one hit kills. He who shoots first wins. Which means that the combat is focused on attacking units you already know about, rather than advancing to area that you don't. This interacts with recon mechanics to favor the side who already has propositioned recon for there position rather than the advancing side who are trying to move recon units into position. Shoot on the move penalties. Most units suffer significant combat penalties when moving, with many not able to fire at all. This gives a major advantage to the defender who's units are still, rather than the attacker who's units are moving Flanking penalties. Many of the best protected units for attacking on the offense are weak if attacked from side or rear. This means that breaking through one part of an opponents line without engaging the rest of it opens your unit to be destroyed from the side. Large starting forces. The players are given enough resources at the start of the game to build a front line, avoiding the need to drip feed in units to stop your opponent building up, prior to the establishment of the front line. Territory based victory system: The standard options for playing these games link held territory to victory. Specific points, located near the center of the maps (so that they force the players together rather than letting them each sit in there own points), must be held, either to accrue points directly towards victory, or to gain resources to buy more units to be able to inflict more damage on the opponent. All of these factors combine to create a situation where combat as much about having the right counter in the right place, and players are unable to generate a big enough blob to meaningfully outweigh the advantages of positioning without leaving themselves open to being destroyed elsewhere on the map. Even if an attacker chooses to create a blob, careful positioning of the defensive units can still allow them to inflict significantly more resource cost in damage than they themselves cost before the defending units are lost, causing the blob to suffer a pyrrhic victory in the overall battle of attrition. Blobs are still occasionally seen, but only when the game is all but won.

text: Thunderbolt is a 90 Power, 100% Accuracy, Electric Special attack.¹ Gigavolt Havoc (Thunderbolt) is a 175 Power, unable–to–miss, Electric Special attack, which requires the Pokémon to be holding the Electrium Z item. Gengar has 130 Sp.Atk, and Mega Gengar (which requires holding Gengarite ) has 170 Sp.Atk. The formula for calculating damage in Generation V onwards is: Damage = ((((((2 × Level) ÷ 5) + 2) × Power × (A ÷ D)) ÷ 50) + 2) × Targets × PB × Weather × GlaiveRush × Critical × random × STAB × Type × Burn × other × ZMove × TeraShield There are a lot of things that don't apply here, or can be ignored. For example neither Gengar nor Mega Gengar are Electric Typed, so there will be no Same Type Attack Bonus (STAB); this is not a Physical attack, so Burn cannot apply; both moves can Crit , so that can be ignored.; etc. So, let's simplify: Damage = ((((((2 × Level) ÷ 5) + 2) × Power × (A ÷ D)) ÷ 50) + 2) × random × ZMove If we assume the exact same Gengar, then Level and IVs will be the same. If we assume the exact same target, then D will be the same. Let's squash all of that into a new variable C that we can ignore. ZMove is the 'bleedover' that a Z-Move or Max-Move gets against protected targets (i.e. 1 against an Unprotected target; 0.25 against a Protected Target for a Z-Move or Max-Move; 0 against a Protected target if this is not a Z-Move or Max-Move). We will run out calculations while assuming an un protected opponent, allowing us to ignore that. (Otherwise, Thunderbolt will do 0 damage) Damage = ((C × Power × A ÷ 50) + 2) × random random will be a random value from 0.85 to 1, chosen anew each time you attack. So, let's plug in some values. Damage(Thunderbolt) = ((C × 90 × 170 ÷ 50) + 2) × random × ZMove = ((306 × C) + 2) × random Damage(Gigavolt Havoc) = ((C × 175 × 130 ÷ 50) + 2) × random × ZMove = ((455 × C) + 2) × random This gives us the following Min and Max damages: Damage(Thunderbolt) = 260C + 1.7 TO 306C + 2 Damage(Gigavolt Havoc) = 386.75C + 1.7 TO 455C + 2 Meaning that the minimum damage from Gigavolt Havoc is roughly 126% of the maximum damage from Thunderbolt, and on average it is about 50% more powerful (well, 48.7%). Note that, from Generation VI onwards, critical hits deal 1.5 times damage — so, a Critical Hit with Thunderbolt will deal about the same damage as a non-Critical Hit with Gigavolt Havoc TL/DR ? Using Gigavolt Havoc on a regular Gengar is almost 50% stronger than using Thunderbolt on a Mega Gengar. The quick way to very roughly calculate it is just to multiply the Power and Atk/Sp.Atk of the move and the Pokémon using it. The largest result will be the stronger attack ¹ While Thunderbolt had 95 Power in Generations I–V, Gengarite was only introduced in Generation VI — the same generation when Thunderbolt was changed to 90 Power

text: For Toriel specifically, missing an attack "on purpose" is considered the same as selecting the "Spare" command. The whole idea here is "to refuse to fight" As for your side question... the requirements for the Pacifist ending are not KILLING anyone during the run. text: Zullie the Witch has a video explaining the key mechanic, namely that jumping disables hit detection for the torso and everything below it, but it does not have complete(*) invincibility frames the way rolling does: In addition: The jumping animation is quicker to recover from than rolling. Jumping naturally transitions into a jump attack, which does more HP and poise damage than a standing attack (but is slower). In contrast, rolling transitions into a rolling attack, which does less damage than a standing attack (but is faster). Some weapons, like shortbows, can attack while jumping without adding much recovery time. Some dragon incantations can be cast while jumping. These add some tactical options unavailable while rolling. Repeated jumping has more "uptime" for its (partial!) damage avoidance than does repeated rolling (Zullie covers this too). A sprinting jump covers considerably more distance than even a light equip load roll, so if a jump will suffice to avoid initial damage, it can carry the player out of range of follow-up damage. Jumping can cause enemy AI to temporarily lose track of the player's location since the player is not on the navigation mesh the AI relies on. Among other applications, jumping can make Malenia's dashes during Waterfowl cover a little less distance. (Don't expect miracles here; this is still difficult to exploit, but can make the difference in the right situation.) That said, jumping takes longer than rolling. At 30 FPS, a jump takes 30 frames, during which 25 provide partial invulnerability, while a (light or medium) roll takes 21 frames, during which 13 provide full(*) invulnerability. Thus, in some cases, rolling will let you take another action more quickly. (Above, I said jumping has quicker recovery. This means there is less time between the end of the jump animation and when you can do something else. But the rolling animation ends sooner, partially offsetting that.) Finally, as noted in a video by Babe1Babe2 : there are certain attacks whose hitboxes are explicitly coded to completely ignore a player that is in the jumping animation. That is the case for the Furnace Golem's single-leg stomp AOE, and is why that attack is jumpable even when on uneven terrain (where the fire graphics often intersect the player's head and arms). So, in summary, jumping provides a variety of situational advantages over rolling, but is typically riskier. Moreover, it requires a lot of trial and error to use effectively, primarily because (without external tools) you cannot see the exact attack hitbox you are avoiding, and of course can't know in advance which attacks magically miss while jumping. (*) Rolling does not provide true invincibility, as there are certain attacks coded to hit even a rolling player. The dungeon chariots' collision is one example, but there are others.

text: You can beat the game and get any ending variation you wish from the first loop. But there's two sections in the endgame that get easier if you're not on the first loop: Your Signalscope will only show frequencies that you've already unlocked by finding an object that emits that signal. Finding the Vessel usually requires you to either track down an object on radio, or have already found it and marked it on your map. Speedrunners bypass this by simply knowing where it is. The helpful pop-up reminding you of the Eye Coordinates will only appear if you've legitimately seen those coordinates on a previous loop. If you only know the coordinates from out-of-game knowledge, you won't get the reminder but they'll still work. Loop counters, not affected by your actions except the number of loops that pass: You can only sleep at a fire to pass the time after the start of the third loop. The equipment in the Probe Tracking Module will count the number of loops elapsed. According to it, the game starts on loop 9,318,054. The easter egg scroll on Giant's Deep shows a "world line divergence" that changes over the course of the loops. The first loop has some important differences until you activate the statue and begin the game proper. You mentioned minor dialogue changes and the possibility to get a game-over by dying, but it's more than that. Time-sensitive events don't happen at all until you trigger the statue. If you somehow get onto your ship and into space without triggering the statue, you'll find that Brittle Hollow doesn't collapse, sand never flows off Ash Twin, and there's no time limit on your exploration. The loop starts from the beginning when you walk past the statue - even if it was broad daylight before, afterwards it'll be midnight on the first day. You usually don't notice this because the museum is indoors.

text: It's called a Companion Cube for a reason: test subjects should become attached. The difference with regular cubes is for measuring emotional responses and ethical choices made by the test subjects, and likely for general reasons of A/B testing, to compare results in test performance between the two different iterations of what is essentially the exact same thing. Similarly with the turrets. Remember that Aperture Science Labs' mission, in Cave Johnson's words, was " throwing science at the wall and seeing what sticks ", i.e. innovate at whatever cost, regardless of moral and ethics. [T]hough why turrets would be made sentient to such a degree that they apparently understand why they're destroyed, I don't know. Possibly because Aperture Science also didn't know, and figured they might as well find out :) The turrets might contain Morality Cores, in addition to or without conscience, or they might just produce random soundbites. They might be cruel experimental or harmless straightforward death machines, but they will impact the test subjects in some measurable way. Apart from the possibility that GLaDOS is simply lying to get what she wants, and always undermining attempts at positive human behaviour (probably to keep the risk of being overthrown as low as possible), those remarks about the Companion Cube tell us more about the history of the test subjects, and GLaDOS' view of them, then about the Weighted Companion Cube itself: While it has been a faithful companion, your Companion Cube cannot accompany you through the rest of the test. If it could talk — and the Enrichment Center takes this opportunity to remind you that it cannot — it would tell you to go on without it because it would rather die in a fire than become a burden to you. To me, this insinuates that test subjects - growing up in complete isolation save for an AI controlling their lives and making snarky comments - lack actual companionship, and grow attached to objects. The rest is just motivational nonsense, that these AIs are so good at spewing (cf. Wheatley). Although the euthanizing process is remarkably painful, eight out of ten Aperture Science engineers believe that the Companion Cube is most likely incapable of feeling much pain. This tells us that even the Aperture Science engineers sometimes have difficulty separating reality from fiction, an indication that they're not much better off than the test subjects (at least, when it comes to oppression—less so when it comes to risking their lives). The staff were actually increasingly used as test subjects, as well, so who knows at which point these statistics (which may be false) were measured. Rest assured that an independent panel of ethicists has absolved the Enrichment Center, Aperture Science employees, and all test subjects of any moral responsibility for the Companion Cube euthanizing process. Unless there is something living or intelligent inside the Companion Cubes, this is just drivel—and likely intended that way: it is an opaque attempt to clear the test subject's conscience, while more likely leading to the very question "is this wrong?". Reverse psychology. That the Companion Cube reappears at the end credits of Portal can also be interpreted in many ways: it might be indestructible, or perhaps Chell has lost her mind, or there are simply lots of copies around. In Portal 2 we find out there are a lot (or at least several) of these Companion Cubes ( Test Chamber 7 : " We have warehouses full of the things "). I believe even in Portal you can already glimpse others behind the walls. In the canonical comic Lab Rat , Rattmann is seen conversing with the Cube, but we know he was delusional, a schizophrenic suffering from hallucinations: It's hard to dismiss all the insinuation, and it can't be proven the Cubes don't have an intelligence or sentience, but to me everything points in the direction of a ploy. For science.

text: Baldur's Gate 3 includes all 12 principal base classes that have been around for at least two editions (the Warlock, being the newest entry, was introduced during 3.5, and turned core for the 4th edition), and have been published as such in the 5th edition Player's Handbook. With the subclasses it's a bit more complicated: BASE CLASS 5E core [2014] BG3 BG3 Patch 8 Barbarian 2: Path of the Berserker, Path of the Totem Warrior 3: Berserker, Wildheart, Wild Magic Path of the Giant Bard 2: College of Lore, College of Valour 3: College of Lore, College of Valour, College of Swords College of Glamour Cleric 7 Domains: Knowledge, Life, Light, Nature, Tempest, Trickery, War 7: idem Extra domain: Death Druid 2: Circle of the Land, Circle of the Moon 3: Circle of the Land, Circle of the Moon, Circle of the Spores Circle of Stars Fighter 3: Champion, Battle Master, Eldritch Knight 3: idem Arcane Archer Monk 3: Way of the Open Hand, Way of Shadow, Way of the Four Elements 3: idem Way of the Drunken Master Paladin 3 (4): Oath of Devotion, Oath of the Ancients, Oath of Vengeance 4: idem + Oathbreaker (but mentioned in DMG 5E) Oath of the Crown Ranger 2: Hunter, Beast Master 3: Hunter, Beast Master, Gloom Stalker Swarmkeeper Rogue 3: Thief, Assassin, Arcane Trickster 3: idem Swashbuckler Sorcerer 2: Wild Magic, Draconic Bloodline 3: idem + Storm Sorcery Shadow Magic Warlock 3: The Archfey, The Fiend, The Great Old One 3: idem Hexblade Wizard 8 Schools: Abjuration, Conjuration, Divination, Enchantment, Evocation, Illusion, Necromancy, Transmutation 8: idem Bladesinging Most of the additional subclasses from the game, including those from Patch 8 , have been published in the supplementary 5E sourcebooks: the Bard subclasses College of Swords and College of Glamour , the Ranger subclass Gloom Stalker , the Sorcerer subclasses Storm Sorcery and Shadow Magic , the Fighter's Arcane Archer , the Monk's Drunken Master , the Rogue's subclass Swashbuckler , and the Warlock subclass Hexblade were published in Xanathar's Guide to Everything , and the Druid's Circle of the Spores and Circle of Stars , the Barbarian's Wild Magic , the Ranger's Swarmkeeper , and the Wizard's Bladesinging in Tasha's Cauldron of Everything . Patch 8's Paladin subclass Oath of the Crown originates in the Sword Coast Adventurer's Guide and the Barbarian subclass Path of Giants in Bigby Presents - Glory of the Giants (as Path of the Giant ). The only two outliers here are the Barbarian's subclass Wildheart , which is Larian's reinterpretation of Path of the Totem Warrior (see e.g. here ), and the Cleric's Death Domain that was added by Patch 8, which is actually a core subclass (from the Dungeon Master's Guide). As for the Artificer base class: this was introduced in the Eberron campaign setting, already during the 3rd edition (but as a Wizard specialization already as far back as 2E), and made its reappearance during the 4th and 5th in non-core rulebooks. As jwodder points out in their answer , it was published in Tasha's Cauldron of Everything , which is a sourcebook (expanding on the Player's Handbook , Dungeon Master's Guide , and the Monster Manual ). Tasha's Cauldron of Everything was published in 2020, whereas development on Baldur's Gate 3 already started in 2016: apart from the exclusion of the Artificer base class from the core rulebooks, this could account for this class not having made it into the game. There is a mod available to remedy that, though.

text: Let's break this down: When you do something with a villager, you generate a "gossip". Like anger, gossip is stored in the NBT of the villager. However, unlike anger, it is a different NBT field and therefore unaffected by forgive_dead_players . That gamerule only affects the angry_at field. In our case, since you are killing villagers, only one type of gossip is relevant: killing a villager. This is the gossip major_negative . From the wiki : Killing a villager increases the value of the corresponding gossip for all villagers whom it has a line of sight inside a box extending 16 blocks from the villager in all coordinate directions. So this is why some of the villagers were affected and other were not, they were witnesses to the carnage! Each major_negative gossip adds adds a 25 gossip "strength". You max out at 100 strength. Each major_negative strength translates to -5 "reputation", so one kill corresponds to -125 reputation. You already max out at 4 kills so that's a whopping -500 reputation. Gossips also decay slowly over time - these particular gossips decay by 10 strength every 20 minutes. So the negative ramifications will last 200 minutes of gameplay or ~3 hours. Villagers also can share gossip during the day so this will cause other villagers to get the gossip but this will reduce the overall gossip strength by 10 per sharing action. You saw the ramifications of negative rep. They increase prices of affected villagers, and golems will attack you. The exact mechanisms are as follows (from the wiki): Iron golems that were not built by players become hostile toward all players whose reputation is -100 or lower with any villager within a box centered on the golem and extending 10 blocks in every horizontal and 8 in both vertical directions. This is why only some iron golems would attack you, they might not be close enough to a traumatized villager. Finally, reputation affects the cost in accordance with this partial formula : price_change = − floor(multiplier * reputation) (I simplified the formula assuming no demand and no hero of the village effect). So you can see how when the reputation goes negative, the price increases by a lot. Depending on the multiplier, -500 reputation can cause the price to increase between +25 emeralds to +100 emeralds (which maxes out to a stack)

text: Quake 3: Ray Traced (Q3RT) was released in 2004 by Daniel Pohl using the OpenRT library to demonstrate real-time ray tracing, but was mostly a research project. Demo: Retrospective research paper by the same author: Title: 15 Years Later: A Historic Look Back at "Quake 3: Ray Traced" Daniel Pohl, Selvakumar Panneer, Deepak Vembar, Carl Marshall . DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.15439/2020F3 Citation: Proceedings of the 2020 Federated Conference on Computer Science and Information Systems, M. Ganzha, L. Maciaszek, M. Paprzycki (eds). ACSIS, Vol. 21, pages 401–412 (2020) Abstract: Real-time ray tracing has been a goal and a challenge in the graphics field for many decades. With recent advances in the hardware and software domains, this is becoming a reality today. In this work, we describe how we got to this point by taking a look back at one of the first fully ray traced games: Quake 3: Ray Traced . We provide insight into the development steps of the project with unreleased internal details and images. From a historical perspective, we look at the challenges pioneering in this area in the year 2004 and highlight the learnings in implementing the system, many of which are relevant today. We start by going from a blank screen to the full ray traced gaming experience with dynamic animations, lighting, rendered special effects and a simplistic implementation of the gameplay with basic AI enemies. We describe the challenges encountered with aliasing and the methods used to alleviate it. Lastly, we describe for the first time the unofficial continuation of the project, code named Quake 3: Team Arena Ray Traced , and provide an overview of the changes over the past 15 years that made it possible to generate fully ray-traced interactive gaming experiences with mass market hardware and an open software stack.

text: Basics of commands and arguments Minecraft's commands system allows players to modify the game in ways besides mining and placing blocks. Commands have different arguments that specify their behavior, such as a selected entity or specified location. For example, the very basic version of /summon has two arguments: An entity to summon A location to summon it at It is important to note that the term “entity” does not only refer to mobs, such as creepers and blazes, but also to other objects that are not blocks, including item frames, paintings, snowballs, and dropped items. Knowing the /summon command's arguments, we can fill them in like so: Example Summon a wither skeleton at the position (0, 80, 0). summon minecraft:wither_skeleton 0 80 0 Relative and local coordinates This, however, is very limiting: what if we wanted to summon an entity at our current position? This is where relative cordinates come in. Relative coordinates are used by putting a ~ instead of a number. To summon a silverfish at my current location, you would do /summon minecraft:silverfish ~ ~ ~ . If you want to add an offset to the location of the relative coordinates, you can do so by typing numbers directly after the ~ . Example To summon a lightning bolt 1 block east, 2.3 blocks up, and 17.914 blocks north: summon minecraft:lightning_bolt ~1 ~2.3 ~-17.914 There are also local coordinates , which use carets ( ^ ^ ^ ). These work identically to relative coordinates, but any offset you use is offset based on the direction that the executing entity is looking. Example Summon a fireball one block in front of the executing entity's crosshairs: summon minecraft:fireball ^ ^ ^1 You cannot mix local coordinates with other types of coordinates. All three axes X, Y, and Z must either all use ^ or not . Target selectors Alongside positional coordinates, which select a position in the world to work with, there are also arguments which select an existing entity within the world to work with. These are named target selectors , but can be called entity selectors as an alternative name. The most basic entity selector is simply the @ sign followed directly by one of five letters. There are five options: @s selects the self (the entity executing the command) @p selects the closest player (to the executing position) @r selects a random player in the world @a selects all players in the world @e selects all entities in the world Target selectors also accept arguments , which are filters to further narrow the amount of entities selected. These range from selecting entities based on what type of entity they are, to filtering based on their location, or even based on their name, or the number of XP levels they have. Selectors are useful if you want to do anything to anyone besides named players: Analysis kill @e[type=minecraft:item] The command is /kill . /kill accepts a single argument, an entity selector that selects which entity to kill. The target selector is @e[type=minecraft:item] . The @e says to start with a list of all entities. Then, type=minecraft:item filters the list to only include item entities and nothing else. All entities that are within the list after filtering will be killed. Therefore: This command will kill all entities of type minecraft:item . This means that all dropped item entities will be killed. It is at this point that it should be noted that commands are case-sensitive. This means that you cannot put a capital letter where there should be lowercase, or vice versa. Many broken commands have been fixed by correcting a misplaced capital or lowercase letter, so make sure you are always very careful about what you are typing. Because there are so many different selector arguments, we won't be covering them all here. If you would like to see what's available, click the link above to view a full list on the Minecraft Wiki. That being said, we have a few important things to note: x= , y= , and z= are special arguments. They are different from the rest in that they are not actual filters, but they instead provide information to other filters. x= , y= , and z= define a position in the world where the other filters are calculated from. Analysis kill @a[x=1,y=2,z=3] The command is /kill . /kill accepts one argument, an entity or list of entities to remove. The target selector is @a[x=1,y=2,z=3] . The only filters present are x=1,y=2,z=3 , defining a position for other filters to be calculated from. But there are no other filters that will utilize this position. Therefore: The target selector @a[x=1,y=2,z=3] does not perform any filtering. This command will kill all players in the dimension that you run this command from. /execute command This is all very useful, but how would I go about summoning a lightning bolt onto every creeper in the loaded world? The /summon command has no entity selector, and I don't want to go around writing down the coordinates of every creeper that I can see. The solution is the /execute command, arguably the most important command in the game because it is able to change the 'metadata' behind a command: who's running it, where they are, which direction they are facing, among other things. The /execute command has several different specifiers we can attach to it to make it run commands in different ways. One of these is the at specifier, which allows us to choose which entities we want to run some command at. In this case, we would want to do /execute at @e[type=minecraft:creeper] run summon minecraft:lightning_bolt ~ ~ ~ . This would run the command "summon a lightning bolt here" from the position of all of the creepers. It is very important to remember who is executing a command and where is the command being executed from. An example of the problems that happen when you forget this is the command /execute at @e[type=creeper] run kill @s . At first glance, this may seem like it will kill all creepers loaded in the world, but it won't. It will kill the entity who runs the command (assuming at least one creeper exists in the world), because @s refers to the self (kill self) and no matter where the command is executed (even if it is at the position of all creepers) @s still refers to whoever is running the command. A fix might appear to be /execute positioned as @e[type=creeper] run kill @s , but this has the same problem: the executing entity is still the entity who runs the command. To fix this, one would run /execute as @e[type=creeper] run kill @s . Now, @s refers to @e[type=creeper] . Of course, one could just do /kill @e[type=creeper] , but this is just an example problem. Item components This is all very well and good, but what if we want to do something more complicated, such as give a random player an unbreakable golden sword with Fire Aspect II which has the bolded, non-italic, dark-red name "Flame Boi" and eats non-gamers? This is where components come in. Components essentially allow you to set certain attributes of items beyond just their location. These consist of tags which have a name and a value . Sometimes, a tag may have multiple or nested values, in which case a list [] (series of values) or compound {} (tags within a tag) will be required. Components can support many other things, but right now we will just use the ones required for the sword. To give the sword, we would use /give @r golden_sword[enchantments={fire_aspect:2},unbreakable={},item_name={text:"Flame Boi",color:dark_red,italic:false,bold:true},lore=["This sword eats non-gamers."]] 1 To break it down, enchantments={...} is a list of enchantments, each of which has a key (the name of the enchantment) and a value (the level of the enchantment) The golden sword has the unbreakable component (the value doesn't matter but needs to be an object), so it lasts long enough to actually kill something. The item_name component specifies the name of the item in the inventory (another object specifying the item components) Finally, lore=[...] is a list of lines of lore to display. Each can be a string, or it can be an object using the same formatted text format as the item name. Additional component tips A very helpful command for learning about item components is /data get entity @s SelectedItem . It tells you all of the components that the item that you're currently holding has. That includes custom names, colors, enchantments, etc. To use it you can craft, find, or /give yourself the item that you want to use, rename and enchant it with an anvil and then hold it. Run /data get entity @s SelectedItem to get all of the components that the item has that you may need to /give yourself an identical item. When using /setblock or /summon rather than /give the syntax used is called NBT (Named Binary Tags) rather than components, and it works in a slightly different way but the same basic concepts still apply. A helpful keyboard shortcut is F3 + I , it will copy a /setblock or /summon command into your clipboard that you can use to set a block, or summon an entity that will be identical to the one you're looking at, including all NBT and block states. You can copy that command into a text editor with Ctrl + C to learn a lot about NBT. If you want a /summon command for a horse with blue leather armor, you can find or /summon a horse, give it blue leather armor, then look at it, press F3 + I and copy the command into a command block, no changes required. You won't need all of the NBT tags in most cases, you can make the command shorter by removing excess NBT tags. Make sure to test the command a few times in the process to make sure you didn't break anything. The keyboard shortcuts provided here are for Windows users, they may be different for mac, linux, or other systems Conclusion If you've read through this and still have a question on how a command works or where to put an NBT tag, item component, or something similar, be sure to read the wiki about that command, or this website which has the data types in NBT, this website which lists the item components in Minecraft, this website which contains information on player NBT, or this website which has information on chunk NBT. NBT and components use syntax very similar to JSON, so several links which may help explain JSON are this , this , this , this , and this . Don't worry if you don't have any programming knowledge/experience or if it is too technical for you: JSON is related to NBT and components in structure but you don't need to know about server-client data interchange or anything like that to use them. This is a good JSON validator, however be wary : JSON and NBT/components are not the same, so valid nbt may be flagged as incorrect JSON because the String identifiers are not enclosed with quotation marks. It's better to figure out why something is broken by hand (tracing braces/brackets, retyping it, checking capitalization...) than be misled by a JSON checker which operates by slightly different rules than NBT. See also How can I fix "unbalanced brackets" in my data tag? However, /tellraw and /title use strict JSON (which can be found here ) so the above tool is very useful for helping create those types of commands. If you have read through this guide and are ready to ask a question about minecraft-commands , make sure to read this guide which gives some pointers on how to ask your question.

text: It's complicated, and I have not developed a complete understanding of it in my trip down this rabbit hole, but I would like to document what I have learned in this answer. First, it's good to understand more precisely what the question is about. When you hover a game on the main store page, you get a little info card about the game: What do those icons mean? Looking at the HTML gives us the file names of those icons: ico_singlePlayer.png , ico_multiPlayer.png and ico_coop.png . If you look at the store page for a game, there is an info section for the game that features those same icons (this one being from Project Zomboid as well): But as you can see, while the info section use the same icons, it does not have a matching number of them, meaning the hover list is not simply a reproduction of the info section. The mystery deepens further when you realise some games show the multiplayer icon without having an info section entry using it (example: Fast Food Simulator), and others show the Co-op icon without a Co-op entry (example: Hearts of Iron IV). The latter one provided a clue. How is Hearts of Iron IV associated with Co-op? The answer turns out to be that Co-op is one of the popular user defined tags for it: This is the only thing relating to Co-op I can find on that game's store page, leading me to believe that the extra icons correspond to tags. Annoyingly the tags don't show these icons, so exactly which tags are associated with which icons is a detail buried in Steam's code base. Cutting out the gory details of all the games I looked at to piece this together, my current model is that this sequence of icons will be, in order: A single player icon, if the game features a single player mode A multiplayer icon, if the game features any form of multiplayer A sequence of zero or more multiplayer icons corresponding to tags and info section entries A sequence of zero or more co-op icons corresponding to tags and info section entries A multiplayer icon, if the game features cross platform multiplayer Points of unclarity being which tags are relevant, and whether there are any other obscure factors that could stick an icon somewhere in the sequence. But this matches all of the games I've looked at, at least. Useful information you can get from looking at this seems to be If it has a single player mode If it has a multiplayer mode If it has co-op If there is more than one multiplayer icon before the co-op section, it seems to feature some sort of non co-op multiplayer If there is a multiplayer icon after the co-op section, it has cross platform multiplayer

text: MCA Selector is a 3rd party tool that can show you what chunks in a world have been generated (and also remove unneeded chunks, which would let you access new chunks without having to travel as far). In order to open a world, you can go to File -> Open World, then select the folder where the world is stored. Example screenshot after loading a world: Once you find a suitable unexplored area to visit, you can hover over it to get the coordinates to travel to. If there are specific parts of your world you want to remove, you can left click regions to select them (scroll in to get more precision, and right click to deselect), then go to Selection -> Delete selected chunks to remove them. Alternatively, you can instead select chunks based on certain criteria. Go to Tools -> Filter and select the desired filters (e.g. chunks that have been inhabited for less than 3 minutes). You can then look at the chunks that are selected (in case any chunks you want to keep are included in it) then delete the chunks once you are happy with the selection.

text: Instead of storing the item in a chest, you store it in a structure by saving a 1×1 structure that consists of just air and the item entities. So the step by step guide is: Throw item(s) on top of a structure block, save the structure with entities (probably as a 1×1×1 sized structure). Change the structure block to load mode. When activated, load the structure at the player's position. Now that you know the plan, let's begin! Step 1: Customize your item So to do this, you're going to need to prepare your item in your inventory. Please observe the following things that you can do to prepare your item: Properties that can be set/changed without using this method You can set the following item properties in a direct command without having to use this method: Default potion effects : Potions can be given as one of the default potions available in the Creative Inventory using data values. CanPlaceOn and CanDestroy : If you want to give an item with these properties alone, you can simply use /give with the JSON components. Properties you can set/change with this method The following properties can be changed within the game using this method: Custom name : Take your item to an anvil. Use the anvil’s rename form to change the item name. Instead of using raw JSON text, use formatting codes to stylize the item name. Some enchantments : Get an enchanted book and combine it with your item in an anvil. You may also use /enchant while holding the item in your main hand. You may not exceed the maximum enchantment level, and you may not enchant items that don't make sense with that enchantment (so no enchanting a fish with Knockback X), but you can use an NBT editor—see below. Filled maps : To give a filled map with custom scale/regions/ to a player, get an empty map yourself, bring it to the region, and activate it. Then place the filled map in the chest. This method is also required to give an empty locator map, because the locator/non-locator data is stored in NBT. Properties that require an NBT editor to be set/changed The following properties can be changed through one-time use of an NBT editor. Follow these instructions to modify any of the below listed properties, and place the item in the chest. The below commands will then work to give an exact copy of the item, even with some properties changed, without requiring use of an NBT editor ever again. Note: The instructions for the NBT editor are out-of-date and will not work anymore. The only method remaining is to also use a structure, however this method has not been posted yet. Lore Unbreakable (won't display on tooltip but still takes effect) Enchantments that an anvil is unable to apply to an item Properties you cannot set/change These are item tags that exist in Java Edition, but the matching NBT tag in Bedrock Edition has not been discovered, or is nonexistent. Feel free to tinker with the NBT tags in an editor, and if you can find any new NBT tags, please comment so I can add to this post! Custom potion effects Step 2: Create the setup Next, we need to create the setup of structures. This is how: Ensure you have positional coordinates shown. If not, run this command in your chat: gamerule showcoordinates true Pick a block on the ground. Any block will do, as long as it is a full block (not a bottom slab, not a chest, not soul sand, etc.). Stand on it, and note the coordinates that are currently in your position. You need a structure void for this. Type the following command in your chat: give @s structure_void Place the structure void on the block of ground you picked in step 1. Throw the item that you have customized onto the ground there too. Ensure it is in the same block as the structure void, not next to it. From this point, you have 5 minutes to complete the next step. Take too long and your items will disappear! Run the following command to save the structure: structure save <name: string> <from: x y z> <to: x y z> true disk false But replace the following items in the above command: Replace <name: string> with a memorable name for your structure. Do not forget it or else you will have to create another one without deleting the old one, taking up memory slowly. How wasteful! Replace <from: x y z> and <to: x y z> with the X, Y, and Z coordinates from step 2. This means that you should have specified the same coordinates twice. Step 3: Set up the commands You only need one command to load the structure onto the player. execute @p[name=target_player] ~ ~ ~ structure load <name: string> ~ ~ ~ If the "Upcoming Creator Features" experiment is turned on for your world, the /execute command's syntax is different, and you should use this slightly different command instead: execute at @p[name=target_player] run structure load <name: string> ~ ~ ~ Replace <name: string> with the name you saved your structure as. Don't remember it? Now you have to go back to step 2 and create a new structure without deleting the old one because you don't remember its name. How wasteful! Once you've set up this command block, run it, and you should see that the item entities are summoned right on top of you so you don't need to run and fetch them.

text: Rocketeers are one of a handful of ARCs that can kill you extremely quickly if you're not careful. With just a light shield, you'll be able to tank one rocket explosion at most before going down. Rocketeers are also quite accurate at close to medium range, so being out in the open with little or no cover is basically a death sentence. If you're particularly unlucky, the Rocketeer will fire multiple rockets in a single barrage, giving you effectively no time to avoid being downed if you're not already in a safe spot. Luckily, there's options for dealing with them. As you've mentioned in your question, showstopper grenades are quite good at knocking them out of the air, at which point you can run up and start smashing their engines with your multitool hammer. (Don't stand directly in front of them, though; they can still fire rockets and will do so if they see a target they can reach.) Similarly, Hornet drivers will have the same effect. You could also of course use a wolfpack grenade, which will usually destroy the Rocketeer outright or at the very least deal a TON of damage, though obviously this is quite expensive. Lure grenades are also a decent option to distract the Rocketeer for a short amount of time while you reposition to a safer location - just throw them away from where you're heading. And finally, for a really unorthodox (and risky) method of defeating them, you could bring a snapshot, hook yourself up to the Rocketeer and climb on their chassis, and then proceed to melee/shoot/deadline mine them while riding them. This renders the Rocketeer unable to retaliate, so it's "relatively" safe assuming you can land the grab in the first place... and that the Rocketeer remains level in the air and doesn't decide to do a barrel roll to throw you off. Outside of that, the most reliable and safest way to deal with Rocketeers is to hide in a location that provides plenty of cover. Short obstacles such as cars are not enough - there needs to be a full wall between you and an explosion to prevent damage. As a result, taking potshots at it from the safety of a building is usually the safest method of defeating them. Of course, if you're not specifically trying to take one down, the best way to deal with a Rocketeer is to not deal with it at all. Try not to aggro it in the first place, and if you do, hide until it resets.

text: How can I breed villagers with mob griefing turned off? You can accomplish this by filling the inventories of the villagers with bread by running this command on an impulse command block with a button for you to activate it: execute as @e[type=minecraft:villager,distance=..5] run data modify entity @s Inventory set value [{count:5,id:"minecraft:bread"}] The distance=..5 makes the command only target villagers less than 5 blocks away, meaning you can build a villager breeding room and place the command block in the middle of that. You can change the distance, of course, or remove it altogether to make every loaded villager ready to breed. Is there a way to turn off creepers destroying blocks (or give a command for a repeating block to kill them as soon as they spawn), while still being able to breed villagers? Yes. You can disable creeper damage by enabling mob griefing again and, in creative mode, set up a repeating command block constantly running this command: execute as @e[type=creeper] run data modify entity @s ExplosionRadius set value 0d This will make the creeper perform no block damage except to entity-blocks like item frames. They will still damage you and other entities though. You need any command blocks to be loaded in-game for the commands to work everywhere in the server. You might be able to set this up (only in Java Edition) by loading the chunk containing the command block with an ender pearl in water over soul sand. If set up correctly, the soul sand constantly will push the ender pearl upward, preventing it from landing. Also see @NODO55's comment about chunk loading, datapacks, and command running :)

text: I'm trying to figure out what to name my custom artwork for non-steam games to get steam to recognize them. Sometime in 2023 (?) Valve changed how Steam identifies art. Instead of hashing the exe and name, it generates a shortcut id and stores it in shortcuts.vdf as 'appid'. Presumably this is so art is preserved when renaming shortcuts. Now you need to read the shortcuts.vdf files and extract the id that it's using. I'd recommend using the Python vdf module to read the vdf file. Here's an example that prints the appids for all of one user's shortcuts: import pprint import vdf shortcut_file_path = "E:/steam/userdata/3230000/config/shortcuts.vdf" with open(shortcut_file_path, "rb") as sf: shortcuts = vdf.binary_load(sf) root = shortcuts['shortcuts'] for key,entry in root.items(): # Uncomment to see everything in each shortcut: # pprint.pprint(entry) exe = entry.get('Exe') appid = entry.get('appid') print(f"{exe} {appid}") See also this steamsync PR for a more comprehensive example for how you could use the appid to control the associated art. steamsync assigns old-style appids when downloading art because it's creating its own shortcuts and adding them to shortcuts.vdf. Old Answer that worked pre-2023 Steam uses two different ids used to load art for non-steam shortcuts. You can ignore the Big Picture specific logic and set the icon as your desired Big Picture art but that icon will also be used in Steam desktop client. Steam Desktop steamgrid figured out how to get a normal shortcut id. They describe the solution as " crc32(exe + appname) + "02000000" , using IEEE standard polynomials" and using exe and appname from shortcuts.vdf. For some reason, steamgrid refers it as the LegacyID, but this is the format for art for steam's redesigned client. This id seems to be unrelated to the desktop shortcut id (which is also used in screenshots.vdf) and unrelated to images in Big Picture mode (which uses the icon field in shortcuts.vdf). UWPHook as a C# implementation to find the id and separate code for the paths . import binascii def get_steam_shortcut_id(exe, appname): """Get id for non-steam shortcut. get_steam_shortcut_id(str, str) -> int """ grid = Path(f"{steam_path}/userdata/{steamid}/config/grid") unique_id = ''.join([exe, appname]) id_int = binascii.crc32(str.encode(unique_id)) | 0x80000000 return id_int Big Picture scottrice/Ice steamgrid figured out how to get a Big Picture shortcut id. They explain: Calculates the filename for a given shortcut. This filename is a 64bit integer, where the first 32bits are a CRC32 based off of the name and target (with the added condition that the first bit is always high), and the last 32bits are 0x02000000. The implementation looks roughly like this (requires pycrc ): # Copyright (c) 2012-2013, 2013 Scott Rice # All rights reserved. MIT License import pycrc.algorithms as crc def get_bigpicture_shortcut_id(exe, appname): algorithm = crc.Crc(width = 32, poly = 0x04C11DB7, reflect_in = True, xor_in = 0xffffffff, reflect_out = True, xor_out = 0xffffffff) input_string = ''.join([exe,appname]) top_32 = algorithm.bit_by_bit(input_string) | 0x80000000 full_64 = (top_32 << 32) | 0x02000000 return str(full_64) See the original for more details/comments. You can see that this is very similar to the normal shortcut id except it has some extra lower bits. Bringing it Together We can put it all together to get the locations for all the art like so: from pathlib import Path import binascii def get_steam_shortcut_id(exe, appname): """Get id for non-steam shortcut. get_steam_shortcut_id(str, str) -> str """ unique_id = ''.join([exe, appname]) id_int = binascii.crc32(str.encode(unique_id)) | 0x80000000 return id_int def get_grid_art_destinations(steam_path, steamid, exe, appname): """Get filepaths for the grid images for the input shortcut. get_grid_art_destinations(str, str, str, str) -> dict[str,Path] """ grid = Path(f"{steam_path}/userdata/{steamid}/config/grid") shortcut = get_steam_shortcut_id(exe, appname) bp_shortcut = (shortcut << 32) | 0x02000000 return { 'boxart': grid / f"{shortcut}p.jpg", 'hero': grid / f"{shortcut}_hero.jpg", 'logo': grid / f"{shortcut}_logo.png", '10foot': grid / f"{bp_shortcut}.png", } import pprint pprint.pprint(get_grid_art_destinations("C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam", '00000000', 'c:\\libraries\\itch\\baba\\Baba Is You\\Baba Is You.exe','Baba Is You')) Here's a complete python implementation .

text: What the internet (Playstation Trophies) says is that: This requires you to get tailed 5 times by other players. There is no notification as to when you are being tailed unless you profile the person who is tailing you. There is also no way to track how many times you've been tailed, unless you look at your players met list on your PlayStation system and spot a tailing that you didn't initiate yourself. If you find yourself not being able to get able to receive any, there is a way to fix it (if you want to call it that). You have to turn off online invasions and reset your notoriety and go back to free roam and then go back in and turn it on again. In free roam, go into options and then online and disable "Online Invasions". Go back to the game so you see the white emblem on the left side of the screen notifying you that the game is saving. Go back to "Online Invasions" and switch it back on. Go back to free roam and do nothing for about 10-20 minutes and then check your recent players met to see if anyone has joined you. If you're good enough, you will be able to spot people coming into your game. If you spot someone suspicious, try pausing the game and if the background is moving on the pause screen, someone is in your game. text: No Thievery only uses the base value of the items, not the price that traders sell it to you. This is easy to verify: Option 1: Check an item's value in your inventory. Easiest to see with something moderately valuable like Resurrection Scroll. Your main character and your companions all start with one, so you have a few spare. A Resurrection Scroll is listed as 120 gold. Sell the item to a vendor. See how much it sells for. The price will be a lot higher than what it said in your inventory. A vendor sells Resurrection Scroll for 300 gold (without Attitude or Bartering adjustments): Try to steal the scroll and see that the value is listed as 120 gold. Option 2 - slightly more roundabout: Start a game with any character. Make sure they have either Thievery or Bartering. On level 2, give them a point in the other skill. Rush through the tutorial section on the ship. Do not do any side activities. Pick up a weapon for the first fight when you get up on the deck. Get to the beach, then follow the road forward to Fort Joy. You should arrive there almost at level 2. text: "Seed" used in this way is from computer programming, and would have been seen by anyone who's merely dabbled with game programming anytime in the past 40 years. In Basic, or C++, or C# (in the Unity3D engine) when you first want to roll dice for a random number you'd read how you first need to pick a seed, in a function like Rand.seed(63) (you have to type out the word "seed"). For text-based games (which includes learning game programming) you'd find a suggestion to print "Enter a seed: " for the player. My point being that anyone who spent a week trying to learn coding for games would definitely have seen "seed" as a thing that somehow determines randomness. Every manual would then explain that computers can't create random numbers, but your "seed" allows them to make a random-looking series of numbers. It would explain how the same seed always generates the exact same series of numbers, so be sure to use a different seed each time(*). Unless you actually want the exact same random rolls; for example, you can "save" a randomly generated dungeon (which we had as early as 1970) by writing down the seed and entering it again. This was in pretty much every manual. Then this trick of remembering the seed to get the same level would have quickly spread to modders. (*)The manual would explain how you can do something like Rand.choose_seed() and have the computer pick one for you, but only after you'd seen and used "seed" so much that you definitely remember it.

text: Elemental effects, and I'm guessing any other dependent mod effects although I'm not aware of any, are determined left to right, top to bottom. So if you want to have e.g. viral (cold + poison) and heat damage on a weapon, you need to have the first mod from the top left be poison or cold, the next be the second element for viral, and the third be heat, otherwise you would end up with cold or poison combining with heat instead. The uncommon variant of elemental mods have Naramon polarity for heat and poison, and Varazin polarity for cold, so for this example, assuming you only have these mods for adding elemental damage and you want to match polarities, you'll want to have an available Varazin slot from left to right, top to bottom before hitting your last Naramon slot. Thus, you may want to swap polarity slots if you want to change the order of mods to take advantage of the order in which they are applied.

text: I realize this question is 4 years old, but here’s an answer for posterity's sake. The problem is not the damage mitigation abilities, but the location of you and your teammates. Put simply, basically every damage mitigation ability in the game is directional. That means if your entire team is stacked in the same location, a single Dva can eat all the damage from all 5 people shooting projectiles at her. On the other hand, if your team is split in such a way that 2 people are shooting at her front and 3 people are shooting at her side, she’ll be taking a lot of damage. For example, you’re on Rialto first point playing against a full team that has damage mitigation abilities: Dva (matrix), Genji (deflect), Mei (wall), Brigita (shield), and Baptiste (immortality field). If your entire team stacks up on the first corner, you could run into a situation where the Dva uses defense matrix. Then, the genji dashes in and uses deflect. Then he backs out, Mei puts down her wall, and by that point Dva has matrix again: All the while, their frontline is getting pocketed by uncontested supports who are able to heal for free. Now if just the soldier takes an off angle and starts shooting the Bap, he’ll probably force some defensive cooldowns from the supports. Additionally, the Genji will be forced to rotate top to help cut off the angle. Now, we’ve got 3 separate people distracted by a single player, and that means the other 4 members on your team are free to start damaging Mei and Dva. Instead of a completely uncontested backline firing heals into their frontline, they are distracted, and it’s very possible that either Dva or Mei die because your team is able to focus fire them between cooldown rotations. All of that was because a single soldier took a single off angle. If you watch high rank streamers, you’ll notice that their teams are frequently completely separated. Soldier is on the high ground firing at the open backline. Widow is down on the bridge free-firing. Zen is charging up volleys and trying to catch a support unawares. Moira might go forward and use her fade to jump back to cover if she gets low. Notice how impossible it is for the defending team to effectively cycle their defensive abilities. Mei might use her wall to cut off the widow sightlines, Genji might jump up to contest the soldier, and Dva is holding down Orisa, but that still leaves Zen and Moira completely uncontested to deal damage. We went from a single Dva preventing your entire team from dealing damage to a complete nightmare for defenders to try and survive against. You don’t have to swap up your team comp to be entirely beam based characters, all you have to do is shoot from a slightly different location from the rest of your team, and it’s gg. Effectively using off angles is perhaps the single biggest improvement you can make in your gameplay to level up.
