text: Let c = 0.000013 (Human, Beaver, Frog), or c = 0.0000195 (Harpy, Lizard, Fox, Bat). Then for each species i: if(r[i] >= t[i]): dr_dt += 0.7 * c[i] * p[i] * r[i] else dr_dt = 0 Here: dr_dt : Change in reputation from resolve per second r[i] : Current resolve of species i. p[i] : Current population of species i. c[i] : Constant associated with each species as above. t[i] : Current resolve target for species i. Example: I have 6 happy beavers at 32 resolve and 8 happy harpies at 20 resolve. There are 6 content humans at 5 resolve. How long will it take me to gain one point? Harpies: 8 × 20 × 0.0000195 × 0.7 × 60 = 0.002184 Beavers: 6 × 32 × 0.000013 × 0.7 × 60 = 0.0017472 Total: 0.0039312 per second. One point takes 254.4 seconds, or 4 minutes 14.4 seconds.

text: TL;DR: The safest way to remove a mod is to load a save from before the mod was installed. Doing anything else will depend on how the mod works. Mod removal mid game is complicated, and has a number of considerations that affect whether it is possible or not. Roughly speaking, we can divide mods into a few different cases: Asset replacers: Mods that only replace textures, meshes, sounds, etc., do not contain an ESP/ESM/ESL file ("plugin file"), and do not replace any vanilla scripts. These mods are generally safe to install and uninstall at any time. If a mesh replacer is installed incorrectly, it may cause the game to crash, but this can be fixed by uninstalling it or correcting the installation. It should not have any lasting effect on the save files. These files may be packed into a BSA archive, and distributed with a plugin file. If the plugin file contains no records (according to xEdit), then it is still an asset replacer, but the game doesn't know that and will display a warning when you try to load a save after removing the plugin file. If you are sure the mod is really an asset replacer and makes no other changes to the game, then this warning may be ignored. Scriptless plugins: Mods that contain a non-empty plugin file, but no scripts of any kind (vanilla or modded), and none of the plugin file's edits are to VMAD ("virtual machine adapter," i.e. script-related) sub-records. These mods may or may not be safe to install or uninstall at arbitrary times, depending on what the mod changes. In most cases, everything the mod adds or modifies will disappear or revert to its vanilla state, which is probably the correct behavior. However, many records can modify the state of vanilla objects (especially the player), and those state changes are not always reverted. If you spent perk points on a modded perk, those might not be refunded. If a magic effect has altered one or more actor values (for you or any NPC), those might stay altered. If a vanilla quest has been significantly modified, it might revert into a broken or unexpected state. And so on. A small number of these problems can be fixed with save unbaker , but there is no general solution because, for most record types, it is not possible to automatically differentiate between "good" and "bad" changes. Save unbaker only handles cases where every change is either "bad" or impossible through normal gameplay. Scripted plugins: Mods that add or modify scripts in any meaningful way. Skyrim automatically copies all scripts into the save file so that it can ensure that scripts resume right where they left off when a save happened. This means that scripts cannot be made to "just vanish" when the mod is uninstalled, but even if you could do that, it probably would not be good enough anyway. Scripts can make arbitrary changes to the game's state, so the only way to determine whether a script is safe to uninstall is to manually inspect it, figure out how it works, and evaluate what is likely to happen when you yank its parent mod out from under it. Scripted mods additionally have all of the risk factors of scriptless plugins, if applicable (i.e. if they edit non-script records according to xEdit). Even though scripts won't instantly vanish, they will usually stop working correctly (or at all) when their parent mod is uninstalled, so you may or may not actually see these scripts do anything problematic once the mod is uninstalled. Some scripted mods provide support for manual uninstallation. This usually consists of undoing whatever state changes the mod is intended to make, shutting down most or all scripts, and then telling the user to save and uninstall the mod. This works if it is implemented correctly, but not all mods provide such a feature (and it is not always feasible to do so anyway). You can use FallrimTools to manually delete orphaned ("unattached") script objects after removing a mod, loading, and saving. For some mods, that is enough to at least get your game into a somewhat stable condition, but it will not undo whatever changes those scripts may have made to your game while the mod was installed. Some of the advice given on the mod description page is considered outdated or questionable , so please do not interpret this link as an endorsement of that advice. I do not know why the mod is flagged as containing "adult content," since I have not seen any adult content in my use of it. SKSE plugins. Mods that contain .dll files and require SKSE. Most of these mods can be safely installed or removed at any time, because they directly hotpatch the engine and make no changes to the save file. If the mod also contains other stuff besides a .dll file (and possibly a .ini file or the like to configure it), then that other stuff may have its own issues (see above). Mods that install custom animations (and do not rely on OAR or a similar engine mod). You will have been told to run FNIS, Nemesis, Pandora, or a similar tool as part of installation (if not, then the mod is not in this category in the first place). You must re-run that same tool again after removing the mod, or else you will get T-posing in some circumstances. If you remove all mods with custom (non-OAR) animations, then you can instead uninstall the output of the tool in question (which you hopefully installed as if it was a mod, rather than letting it dump files straight into your game installation). Most of these mods also have scripts, so see above, but the animations themselves do not otherwise pose any problems for uninstallation. Make sure that neither the player nor any NPC is in the middle of any custom animation before uninstalling whatever mod provided that animation. Many modders and users have developed rituals for making a "clean save." In the context of certain specific record edits, some of these rituals do have useful effects, but there is no general means of making a clean save other than loading a save from before the mod was installed. Here are some examples of specific rituals you might see recommended, and the extent to which they work: Making a save in an interior cell (i.e. any indoor area), uninstalling the mod, loading a save (ignoring the warning), and then saving and loading again. This clears the missing plugin warning on game load, but does not accomplish much else. If a mod edits any exterior cells (outdoor areas), it may be a bit safer to do the first load in an interior cell rather than an exterior cell. If the mod also edits interior cells, then it is probably wise to select an interior which the mod does not touch. As before, but wait 30 (in-game) days before saving and loading again. This causes all cells that respawn to do so, even if their location is cleared (in practice, most cells respawn, but not player homes and a few other places ). It may also cause some encounter-related caches to clear (encounter zones are used to randomly generate enemies of an appropriate level in most dungeons and much of the wilderness). If a mod only edits respawning cells and/or encounters, then this probably removes most or all of its edits from the world. As before, but edit a game setting to some low value, wait a short period of time, then edit the game setting back up to 30 days. This is, as far as I can tell, a complete placebo, because the game setting in question is only evaluated when you enter a cell. If a mod recommends doing something like this, you should wait the full 30 days instead, and don't bother fiddling with your game settings. It is probably not safe to edit e.g. the GameDaysPassed global to manually advance the time. This is because several game systems expect that they can schedule events to happen at specific in-game times, and these events will be skipped if you change the time without explicitly Waiting or Sleeping. More elaborate schemes involving multiple saves, multiple loads, etc. I can't think of anything that would be accomplished by something like this, but that doesn't prove that it is useless in every conceivable circumstance. Scripts can receive an event when the game is loaded, so it is not entirely impossible that some specific mod might respond to a save-load by doing something that happens to be useful. But I don't think this is likely to work as a general means of cleaning save files.

text: Based on your self-answer , I would like to add few more tips. When fighting against Grey Prince Zote, the best advice I can give you is to try and stay as close to him as possible so that you know what he's up to, while trying to keep a safe distance because, as you mention, his nail has a very long reach. It's counter intuitive because staying far away from the boss/threat should make you safe, but if the boss is out of your line of sight, you have no idea what they'll do next. Specifically in the case of Zote, keeping him in your line of sight helps in 3 kind of situations (timestamps based on your video): At 1:11 in your video, he does his huge leap then slam his nail onto the ground. Even if you stand very far, this leap will get close enough to surprise you, and since you don't see him making the initial leap, it can take you by surprise, like at 1:28, whereas if you're at point blank like at 0:45 and 0:56, you can dodge it nearly the same way as one of his normal jumps. Another danger is when he "teleports" into the sky like at 0:58. If you're too far, you won't know he's going to fall into you unless you recognise his scream, whereas if you keep him in range, you will notice him disappearing, allowing you to mentally prepare to dodge him from above. You probably noticed you can tell from which direction he's falling based on where the scream comes from (left, right, or right where you are). And in the case of his frantic swing, you need to find a middle ground: if you stand too close, the moment he raises his nail with its long reach, you may be hit even before you get to dodge it. But if you stand too far, he may have too much acceleration for you to have enough time to dodge it. As you can see at 1:16 in your video, he starts out slowly and quickly becomes very fast. But every time you go to the other side, he has to resume accelerating. In that kind of situation, what I did was very similar to you: jump, attack downward to bounce off of him, then land safely on the other side, and proceed to jump right away then repeat until he trips and fall. Okay I just took the time to try and fight him again, and here's what I noticed. When Zote is about to chase you with his nail, you can notice he needs a few moment before he starts moving; let's call it the acceleration period. Once he's done accelerating, he's charging towards you very fast, which makes it harder to dodge him if you don't see him coming. The trick here is: when you dodge him/jump over him and land on the other side, you can see he still has some momentum when he turns around to try and keep chasing you, a bit like a car doing a U-turn: it needs to stop before it can go the other way. Because of that, after jumping over him, you have 1 second to land and proceed to jump again to the other side, which is more than enough to safely avoid his charging (see the following video at 0:47): However, if possible, you need to avoid getting cornered on the sides of the map, because whenever he hits the wall, he brakes instantly, allowing him to resume charging the opposite direction right away, preventing this strategy from working: In this case, it's best to stick with what you found and keep bouncing off of him by slashing downward.

text: Using different BIL (windbomb) methods is mostly preference, but there are some benefits to using each. The square bomb has a flatter surface area, thus giving you more room for error. The round bomb has a rounded surface area which means you need to hit it more directly into link. For this reason, most people use the round bomb first so as to impact the square bomb into link. The square bomb is used first in some setups with the main one being off the ground, such as the backflip setup, in which you use a stump/elevated surface to get bullet time from a backflip towards the square bomb, pulling out the circle bomb midair and detonating the square, with a consistent circle bomb impact into you. People who learn the stump method first will often use the square bomb first as it feels more natural, or use the square first as their tutorial did so. I also believe that square first can be better for vertical gliding BILs as you will have a better diagonal than the square's corner, because every direction from the circle is equal, you can go up or down further. Using the circle first is much easier for ledge and spider BILs, and I will recommend that you start using it first. I would say for learning BIL, you will want to start with the spider, then ledge, followed by horizontal gliding BIL. The vertical gliding BIL you learn when you have higher stamina and you have the stamina to chain a vertical gliding into a horizontal gliding, just to be able to get anywhere faster, scale cliffs, or just glide longer.

text: If you could put shulker boxes inside each other, you could actually have an infinite amount of items inside one shulker box, as long as you have loaded shulker boxes inside each other. Now here we are going to solve how many items you can actually fit into one inventory. There are 36 inventory slots with one available slot for shields, arrows, maps, totems of undying, etc., and 4 slots for armour . First, lets add up the armour and shield slots. That bring us up to 5 items . Now, if we fill a shulker box up with items, we can fit up to 27 slots, with 1728 items . Because there are 36 spaces in your inventory , we have to multiply the amount of items in the shulker boxes by 36. By doing that, we can get 62,208 items . If we include the shulker boxes themselves, we can fit up to 62,244 items and then finally we can add the remaining 5 slots from shields and armour. This totals up to a grand total of 62,249 items that you can fit into your inventory at one time . Note: I'm not adding a shulker box into the off-hand because you are playing Minecraft Bedrock edition, but if you do want to add a shulker box into your off-hand, you can get up to another 1729 including the extra shulker box. This leads to another grand total of 63,978 items .

text: At the time this question was asked, the answer would have been affected by even more randomness, because there used to be a random tick delay after mining most ores which was removed on December 7th 2022 . Official messaging indicating that: Get your Pickaxes at the ready, because we’ve removed the delay after Mining Copper, Tin, Coal, Blurite, Silver, Volcanic Ash, Gem Rocks, Gold, Mithril, Lovakite, Adamantite, Clay, Salts, Runite and Amethyst. Phew, we can take a breath now. First, the factors affecting your chance to obtain ore from mining are as you noted, with one addition: Pickaxe material, which determines how many ticks there are between rolls to obtain an ore Mining level, which determines what ores you can mine and the odds of obtaining an ore when rolling. Note that any bonuses to mining level such as the hidden Mining Guild boost will increase your odds of obtaining an ore based on your effective level, but not allow you to mine new ores. Ore being mined, which also determines the odds of obtaining ore when rolling. Mining enhancers , which can add a chance to obtain an extra ore when rolling, among some other effects that do not directly impact ore rates. With these factors in mind, here's my stab at an actual formula for ores per hour. First, variables, constants, and their sources: There are 0.6 seconds per game tick : The game tick, also known as the server cycle, is the fundamental unit of time used in Old School RuneScape, equal to 0.6 seconds. All actions that require server processing are governed by this value. Each pickaxe rolls to obtain ore from a rock every n ticks, where n is determined by the specific pickaxe being used . Note that the Dragon, Infernal, 3rd Age, and Crystal pickaxes actually have a chance to take one fewer tick, but we'll use the average as the wiki does. Better picks do not increase mining odds, only frequency. Higher-level pickaxes grant more frequent opportunities to obtain an ore from a rock but do not impact the success rate of doing so. 3 ticks by default, 1/6 chance to be 2 ticks [for the Dragon, Infernal, and 3rd Age pickaxes]. 3 ticks by default, 1/4 chance to be 2 ticks [for the Crystal pickaxe]. And there is a certain chance to obtain an ore per roll, which depends on the mined ore and your mining level. For simplicity, we'll assume that this percentage of rolls will yield an ore. Unfortunately for our purpose, while there are formulas for each rock type that determine your percent chance to obtain an ore on each roll, these formulas are not publicly known! Some have been derived and posted on the wiki , but all of them seem to be unrelated to one another. For example, your odds of obtaining Silver ore each roll at level 20 is 60/256 (23.44%), and 199/256 (77.73%) at level 99, with increases in those odds at every level. However, for Runite, your odds are 17/256 (6.64%) at level 85, and 19/256 (7.42%) at level 99, with increases every 6 levels (at 91 and 97). In short, we just have to look up the odds for each ore at each mining level. So the formula, which assumes perfect mining: time spent mining t / 0.6 seconds per tick = ticks ticks / ticks per roll (from pickaxe) = rolls rolls * ore chance per roll (from level and ore) = expected ore yield expected ore yield * (1 + odds of obtaining an extra ore per roll) = actual ore yield ((t time spent mining / 0.6 seconds/tick) / (n ticks/roll)) * p1 ore chance * (1 + p2 extra ore chance) = ore yield So for example, if you mine iron with level 55 mining , you have a 237/256 (92.58%) chance to obtain an ore. If you mine iron for an hour using a Rune pickaxe (3-tick), you'll roll for ore 2000 times and obtain an ore 92.58% of the time, and so expect to obtain ~1850 ores. If you've completed the Varrock easy diary and use the Varrock armour 1 while mining, you have a 10% chance to get an extra ore on each successful roll, so you'd expect to obtain ~2035 ores instead. ((1hr / 0.6seconds/tick) / (3 ticks/roll)) * 237/256 ore chance * (1 + 0.10 extra ore chance) = ~2036 ores per hour. Not bad! Except this doesn't consider banking time, or how quickly your inventory will fill up with non-ore items like gems (especially with bonuses from the amulet of glory !) or unidentified minerals from the Mining Guild . To consider these factors in a general way, we can introduce an efficiency percentage , which will be the percent of time spent actively mining during a period of time in which you're generally participating in mining but leave occasionally to bank your loot. I can't provide a direct way to calculate this percentage, as it will depend on how quickly you can navigate to the nearest bank and how often your inventory fills up. But it's easy to introduce: ((t time spent mining / 0.6 seconds/tick) / (n ticks/roll)) * k efficiency * p1 ore chance * (1 + p2 extra ore chance) = ore yield So if we continue the prior example, sneak into the Mining Guild with a Spicy Stew boost of +5 , and assume that 20% of our time is spent banking (or conversely, 80% of our time is spent mining), we can take advantage of the cluster of three iron rocks and being steps from a deposit box . In this circumstance, and adjusting for our 80% efficiency, you'd expect to obtain ~1628 iron ore. Well, except that our effective level is now 62 because of the invisible +7 boost to mining from the mining guild , so our ore chance goes up to 255/256 (99.61%) . Re-entering this into the formula to update our result: ((1 hour spent mining / 0.6 seconds/tick) / (3 ticks/roll)) * 0.80 efficiency * (255/256) ore chance * (1 + 0.1 extra ore chance) = ~1753 ores per hour. Given the iron mining guide from before defaults to 1700 iron ore per hour for calculating your profit, I'm reasonably confident this figure is accurate to the given circumstances.

text: In more modern Minecraft, that is somewhat possible, but you need datapack trickery. The setup: Dispensers can't place most blocks, but they can use spawn eggs, spawning whichever entity those spawn eggs contain. Spawn eggs can have the entity_data data component ( EntityTag NBT tag in 1.20.4 and lower) that allows you to overwrite the spawned entity by specifying an entity id . Minecraft has a falling_block entity ( FallingSand in 1.10 and lower). The game itself uses it for, well, falling sand as well as other gravity-affected blocks (including detached dripstone and scaffoldings), but using the BlockState:{Name:...} entity NBT, you can have any block fall from the sky (that's how Only One Command machines used to work before datapacks were introduced and made them obsolete). So taking all of this together, you need to fill your dispenser with spawn_egg[entity_data={id:"falling_block",BlockState:{Name:"cake"}}] items instead of ordinary cakes. It should be mostly safe to simply replace all cakes inside of player inventories with cake spawn eggs. The only side effect is that freshly placed cakes act like gravity blocks, but behave normally once they have landed. So what you can do is attach a technical advancement to crafting a cake, that runs a function containing the following commands (needs adjusting for 1.20.4 and lower, and assuming that the advancement is named craft_cake and placed in the cake namespace): clear @s minecraft:cake 1 give @s minecraft:spawn_egg[minecraft:entity_data={id:"minecraft:falling_block",BlockState:{Name:"minecraft:cake"}},minecraft:custom_model_data={strings:"spawn:cake"},minecraft_custom_name={text:"Cake",italic:false}] advancement revoke @s cake:craft_cake You can run the function manually to change cakes in your own inventory, if desired. I've set it up such that doing so turns one cake at a time into a cake spawn egg. You'll also want to include a resource pack (ideally as a world resource pack in Singleplayer, or server resource pack if on a server) that retextures the spawn egg item into a cake if the custom_model_data property is set like in the command, so that it's only visible through Advanced Tooltips (which will show the spawn egg item ID). Side note: I don't have Minecraft at hand right now, so I wasn't able to test my setup. Also, for some reason, literally no source in existence would tell me the item rarity of cake, so you likely need to adjust the item name color in the custom_name component.

text: If you don't know who has each diamond Step one Give each player a unique scoreboard ID. See this related question for how to do that. Step two Run the following command in a repeating, always active command block: execute as @e[type=item,nbt={Item:{id:"minecraft:diamond"}}] run data merge entity @s {Item:{components:{"minecraft:custom_data":{Unclaimed:1b}}}} This gives each diamond item on the ground a custom Unclaimed tag, allowing you implement Step 3 without 30+ command blocks per player Step three Once for each player who could be playing the map, run in a repeating command block: clear @a[scores={Id=1}] diamond[custom_data={Unclaimed:1b}] 1 and then, in a conditional chain command block that the repeating command block is pointing to /give @a[scores={Id=1}] diamond[custom_data={PlayerOwns:1b}] Repeat this for each player, using scores={Id=2} and PlayerOwns:2b for the second player and so on. Step four Now that each diamond has a tag describing whose it is, you can use the technique described in In2itivity's answer to determine who put a diamond in the chest. This has a known bug that if Alice puts a diamond in a container, and then Bob takes the diamond out of the container (and never drops and picks it up again), the diamond is still interpreted as belonging to Alice -- but I actually like that if I understand what you're doing correctly; if you stole someone else's diamond from a chest instead of mining your own, that means you're trying to cheat… karma! If you want a more seamless experience, you may want to interest yourself in player inventory modification . With the method above, the diamond is visibly replaced by a different one, you can use this to make a seamless replacement.

text: No, not necessarily at Y 127 According to Minecraft Wiki , When lightning is to strike, random X and Z coordinates within the chunk are chosen, and the block just above the highest block that is liquid or obstructs movement is chosen for the lightning strike. If a lightning rod is nearby, it strikes the rod instead. Then if there are any living entities that can see the sky in a 3×h×3 region from 3 below the target block up to the world height, one such entity is selected at random and the lightning target is moved to the block the entity stands in. The target block is checked again for the following conditions: Target block can see the sky. Rain (not snow) is falling in the target block. Thus, lightning does not naturally strike within cold biomes or biomes where it does not rain. If these conditions pass, lightning strikes. That means it will strike as long as the block can see the sky (the path of the lighting isn't impeded by another block). So if you build a roof at Y=256, and it's the highest non-air block in that column, then yes, lightning will hit that roof instead of your house below. Building a glass roof at Y=256 will protect everything underneath, as long as it's the highest surface. You don’t need to build it at Y=126 — that’s not a special lightning layer. If you want more control, use a lightning rod : It attracts lightning within a ~64-block radius (Java). Place it somewhere safe, and it’ll redirect lightning strikes away from flammable structures. TL;DR: No, lightning doesn’t strike only at Y=127. It hits the highest block in the column. A roof at Y=256 will absolutely stop lightning from hitting your house below.

text: To collect honey, you need to get a special jar from the questgiver by talking to her. Things to know, #1: The jar is valid within a limited quest area only; if you cross its border even a little, the jar and its contents disappear. Try to find the border first before losing honey. To fill the jar, you need to get up to the beehives, and "use"/frob them. Different hives give different amounts of honey; an status icon should appear with a number on it. But if you go for some achievements, you need to activate/use/frob the hives, regardless of the honey. You can't do that without the jar. So this helps with the achievements, while frustrating players who don't know the special mechanics here. Depending on your other quests, a bee called Ms. Buzz can be found who asks you to give her the honey instead. If you do, she buzzes off and can be found in the "Queen's Confidence" location later. It's related to a different quest; no effect to the honey collection other than that. Now, the jumping puzzles can be quite taxing. There's a shortcut here, but it's kind of a spoiler: You can use the Jade Bot Glider Booster skill on "6" from EoD. Run up the hill a bit, jump downwards to glide, use booster to gain height. text: Here’s an updated and polished version of your full Stack Exchange answer with that extra detail worked in: Answer: Turns out the issue was caused by syntax errors in my not_mob.json and raycast_pass.json files after updating to Minecraft 1.21.5. So if you’re running into similar issues after the update, make sure to: ✅ Check your tag JSONs for outdated names ✅ Update your datapack folder paths to match the new singular form Once I made those changes, everything worked smoothly again.

text: "a bedrock edition guy"'s answer is right on paper, but there is an easier way to do it. Bedrock has a /structure command that will help. First, /give @s structure_block /give @s structure_void Then, place paintings until you get the one you want, cover it in Structure Voids (they don't replace blocks when loaded, so an accidental load in the wrong place will be safe), then name and save the structure. Remember the name, you will need it again. Then, if you want to spawn the painting, run (without [] characters, those are for clarity, not part of the command) /structure load [name of your structure goes here] [coordinates go here] For paintings bigger than 1x1, it's the lowest value of each coord. So a painting that stretches from [2, 4, 3] to [2, 6, 1] would use 2, 4, 1. If you want to place the painting in a different direction than it was saved, additionally specify one of the options displayed by auto-complete after typing the coords. The options are clockwise, and the coord used is the lowest of each of the coords of the rotated structure, not the unrotated structure. So a painting that would go from [2, 2, 3] to [2, 2, 4] unrotated, but [2, 2, 3] to [2, 2, 2] rotated 180 degrees would be spawned with /structure load [name of your structure goes here] 2 2 2 180_degrees

text: Wilds works more like World. Basically, cutscenes/transitions cannot be shared, but the actual monster fight/completion can. Generally the quests are broken out into an introductory exploration/cutscene sequence, then once the actual monster fight starts it becomes a full fight like any other, then there's a possible post-fight cutscene. e: The linked party answer is better, use that one instead. It allows you to join once you're in the fight, without explicitly abandoning the quest. If you want to do as much as possible multiplayer, you need to: Start the story quest solo Progress past the cutscenes until you get to the monster fight Wait for SOS flares to become available At this point it is possible to proceed with multiplayer. You can either: Have everyone abandon and then post the quest as normal, or Have everyone except one person abandon, and have the one staying in fire a SOS flare. Everyone else should join the SOS. On completion, everyone should get the completion recorded and be able to progress past the quest. I recommend creating a private squad lobby before doing this, to make it easier to join the hunt-in-progress. Yes, it's incredibly janky. Sadly, from World experience, they're unlikely to change this.

text: I want to progress as far into Elite Levels as I can. With that said, this is how you tackle dojos: Double Dragon Build Rings: Weapon Crit, Weapon Damage/Attack Speed, Passive Crit Passives: Vampire Ring, Unstable Laser, Unstable Beam Gadget: Sticker, Capsule, Pepper Spray OR Monster Taser Weapon: Techno Fists Strategy Just kite them, avoid getting hit and time your stuns (Pepper Spray or Monster Taser) with Techno Fists' super attack to keep them moreorless perpetually slowed. Constantly attack, and time your Pepper Spray OR Monster Taser with the passive. Dodge where necessary. Crowd Control Build Rings: Cooldown, Passive Crit, Gadget Crit Passives: Unstable Lightning, Unstable Lazer, Explode-o-matic Gadget: Snow Globe, Vitamin OR Smart Fireworks, Pepper Spray Weapon: Smart Portal Note: Ensure Pepper Spray is in the right-most gadget spot, as pictured. Strategy Your smart portal is not going to do a lot of damage, but your Pepper Spray and Snow Globe will. However, don't pop all two of them at the same time. Your goal is to aggro all the enemies and keep them perpetually slowed, and obviously avoid getting hit while kiting them around. As long as you can do that, keep attacking and time your Pepper Spray and Snow Globes to keep them perpetually damaged and slowed, you should be good. Pop your Missiles or Vitamins as soon as they come off cooldown to increase your DPS/heal up (if you're unable to kite them properly). Helping Hands "The Pet Build", also the best in single enemy DPS. Build Rings: Pet Attack Speed/Damage, Pet Crit, Pet Health Passives: Chicken-o-matic, Unstable Laser, Healthy Snacks Gadgets: Vitamin, Life Jacket, Shelldon Weapon: Buzz-kill Strategy Use Shelldon to tank, and Life Jacket to protect yourself/Shelldon. Pop your vitamins as often as possible, while using Buzz Kill to build up chickens and buzzes (your DPS from the weapon). Taking Hits Build Similar build to Crowd Control , but replace your Vitamins with Super Loud Whistle. Rings: Cooldown, Passive Crit, Gadget Crit Passives: Unstable Lightning, Explode-o-matic, Unstable Laser Gadgets: Globe, Whistle, Pepper Spray Weapon: Portable Portal Note: Ensure Pepper Spray is in the right-most gadget spot, as pictured. As soon as your Snow Globe wears off, then time the Pepper Spray, Snow Globe and your Portable Portal's super attack (aka. Pepper Spray #2). If the enemies target the Plump Spirit, you can aggro them back with Super Whistle. This is especially important in Hard and Nightmare modes as you won't be able to sustain the DPS alone without dying. Target Priority Build Rings: Cooldown, Gadget Crit, Passive Crit Passives: Unstable Lightning, Unstable Laser, Unstable Beam Gadgets: Boom Box, Cool Sticker, Vitamins Weapon: Spin-sickle Strategy Basically spin on each group one by one and popping your Boom Box just before the Blower activates his horn (it's basically a Super Loud Whistle). text: First, "Run Game" to make sure the game is loaded into the iframe and the data is available in the browser. Open browser dev tools on the webpage with the game ( Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + i , F12 , right click -> Inspect). Chrome: "content overrides" must be enabled in the dev tools settings ( F1 or Shift + ? while focused in dev tools window), under Preferences -> Persistence header -> Enable local overrides . Disable this after using. In dev tools go to: Chrome: Sources -> Page tab on top left -> drill down: top -> index.html -> html-classic.itch.zone -> html/12787019 -> js -> right click rmmz_managers.js -> select Override content -> select folder to store custom local version of file -> press Allow in popup at top of browser. Firefox: Debugger -> Sources tab on top left -> drill down https://html-classic.itch.zone/html/12787019/index.html -> html-classic.itch.zone -> html/12787019/js -> right click rmmz_managers.js -> Add script override -> select folder to store custom local version of file. Edit the local copy of rmmz_managers.js following below. Overriding loadObject will cause it to log when starting the game, which will require restarting the game to get additional logs. Overriding saveObject will instead cause it to log when saving. loadObject StorageManager.loadObject = function(saveName) { return this.loadZip(saveName) .then(zip => this.zipToJson(zip)) .then(json => { console.log(saveName, json) return this.jsonToObject(json) }) }; saveObject StorageManager.saveObject = function(saveName, object) { return this.objectToJson(object) .then(json => { console.log(saveName, json) return this.jsonToZip(json) }) .then(zip => this.saveZip(saveName, zip)); }; Now, reload the page with the game and press "Run Game" again to cause the browser to load the override, and go to the Console tab in browser dev tools. After loading or saving, as chosen, it will log the name of the file + the save data to the Console where you can highlight and copy it (or just press Copy if it's a lot of data, like the file N saves), then paste that in a file somewhere you'll remember like your desktop with a proper name so you know which of the 3+ files it is ( config , global , file0 - autosave, file1 ... fileN - manual save). Go to save-editor.com and one by one upload each JSON file and use the "File Encoder" option of the site to convert it to a .rmmzsave file and then manually download it. Finally, go to the folder containing the offline/PC version of the game (and make sure the game is not running - didn't test with it running, but to be safe), go into the save folder, then delete/move/backup existing data if desired and move the newly-converted save data in, start the game, and if done properly the save data will show up when you press "Continue". If not done properly it will just ignore the save files and there will be nothing to continue from. This would also occur if the online version vs offline version don't match, as RPGMaker does check the engine versions when it first starts. RPGMaker Save Editor is an Electron app which can do this locally. Not very pretty, but it seems to be functional. I don't plan to maintain it, but have updated the app to the latest Electron and submitted it to the author.

text: Different damage types are affected by different resistances. From the Cyberpunk wiki : Physical Damage is the default damage type for Melee and Ranged Weapons, such as the Baseball Bat and Liberty. Physical Damage is mitigated by Armor. Chemical Damage has a chance to cause a Poison effect to a target. Chemical Damage is mitigated by Chemical Resistance. Electrical Damage has a chance to apply a Shock effect, that deals an instant large hit of additional Electrical damage. Electrical Damage also has a chance to cause an EMP . Electrical Damage is mitigated by Electrical Resistance. Thermal Damage has a chance to apply a Burn effect, that deals Thermal damage over time. Thermal Damage is mitigated by Thermal Resistance. Those effects are: Poison is inflicted by Chemical damage, which can be dealt by various weapons or the Contagion Quickhack. A target afflicted by Poison will receive Chemical damage over a short duration, a reduction in Armor, and is unable to sprint. EMP briefly deactivates or severely limits the combat effectiveness of Mechs, Drones and Robots while also dealing additional damage to these types of Enemies. EMPs have a chance to be triggered by Electrical damage or by the Short Circuit Quickhack Burn is inflicted by Thermal damage, which can be dealt by various weapons, the Overheat Quickhack, and exploding barrels and devices. A target afflicted by Burn will suffer high Thermal damage over a short duration. Certain enemies are more resistant/vulnerable to damage types. For example, all robots and drones take more damage from electrical attacks while being resistant (or even immune) to poison. From the story point of view, there is no difference in what type of damage your cyberware causes - e.g. you can use the electric Gorilla Arms to open a locked door just as efficiently as a plain physical one.

text: To pair your controller with a second Puck or Steam Machine and use it as a second device, you need to ensure that your controller is turned on in its second pairing slot. When turning on your controller, hold down L1 + A and then (while the other buttons are still held) press Steam , to go into its second pairing slot (this appears to be the information the Steam help page is missing). Your controller will make a different to normal noise when it turns on; the different noises are meant to help denote what device the controller is going to attempt to pair to. Then follow the pairing instructions in the question. The controller will now pair to the device and use the Puck/Steam Machine as the 2nd device. You can then see the 2 paired devices in your Steam Settings, under Controller, while the Controller is turned on: In the future, you should hold the relevant buttons when turning on the controller to connect to the correct device. R1 + A , Steam to connect to your primary device (the Steam Machine in this example), and L1 + A , Steam for the secondary (the Puck attached to the PC in this example). The controller will, however, remember what pairing slot it was last in if you simply turn it on with the Steam button. So, if you were last using your controller with your Puck, turning it on with the Steam button will mean it'll attempt to pair to the second device (the Puck). Again, the noise the controller makes will help you identify what device it will try to pair to. You need to turn the controller off (hold the Steam button), and and turn it back on with the correct button combination to change pairing slot. Note, you can also use R1 + B , Steam to enable Bluetooth pairing. Of course, pairing with Bluetooth doesn't follow the above instructions as this doesn't use a Puck.

text: I ran into this problem and couldn't find a solution online. Later I managed to find a fix so I'm sharing it here in hope it can help other Blizzard game players playing on NVIDIA GeForce Now. This is for people with multiple battle.net accounts, playing Blizzard games using NVIDIA GeForce Now, needing to switch battle.net accounts on GeForce Now, who have trouble using the automatic login feature to log into the correct battle.net account as they have set, where GeForce Now may be logging them into a previously connected battle.net account. After trial and error, here's how I fixed it: First disconnect any Battle.net account from your GeForce Now settings. Then in your browser go to "account.battle.net" and log into your old account. On the left side menu, go to "Connections", and you should see this: "NVIDIA GeForce Now" is in Connections, as well as "Authorized Applications" down bottom. You want to remove both of these from your old account. (After that, I waited a few moments. I'm not sure if this is necessary, but I wanted to be on the safe side. In fact I would recommend waiting a few moments between some of the steps just to prevent any possible syncing issues) Log your old battle.net account out from the browser, and log your new one in. Go to GeForce Now and connect your new battle.net account like normal. Launch the game from GeForce Now. Once the game window opens, you should already be logged out of any battle.net accounts, and will be prompted to connect one. You just connect your new one there. Hopefully this can help people!

text: It's called "wintrading", or "teaming". These players are the lowest level of wintrading. Wintrading is split into a hierarchy of 3 levels (from highest to lowest): Pushers (going 90k+) Organized (no need for spinning, but not competitively) Noobs (they spin around) So how does this work? This works becuase they have huge discord servers with usually 1k+ people. They send out battle cards for the day, a specific configuration for their title, emotes, and profile icons in their battle card for solo showdown, so that they recognize each other. Organized and Pusher wintraders don't have to spin because they recognize each other from the battlecard and names. Then, they also set up the VPN to be in the same place so that they have a higher chance of being in the same lobby. Additionally, they try to push brawlers near the same trophy count to increase it even more. Finally, the owner sends out multiple @everyone pings during one specific time period for everyone to load in during that time period, called waves. Sorry for the late reply, but hope this helps!
